questions.question: Before changing lanes, motorcycle riders should turn their heads to look over their shoulders. Why?

options.text: Motorcycles have blind spots, just like other vehicles.
It helps catch the attention of other drivers.
Mirrors do not work well.
It helps make eye contact with other drivers.

questions.correctAnswerText: Motorcycles have blind spots, just like other vehicles.
questions.explanation: Motorcycles have blind spots that mirrors cannot show. Always turn your head to check for vehicles or hazards in your blind spot before changing lanes.

questions.question: What does making eye contact with other drivers mean?

options.text: It is the best way to know they see you.
It is not worth the effort.
It does not mean they will give you the right of way.
It guarantees they will give you the right of way.

questions.correctAnswerText: It does not mean they will give you the right of way.
questions.explanation: Never assume eye contact means a driver will give you the right of way. Drivers often look directly at motorcyclists but do not see them.

questions.question: Where do most conflicts happen between motorcycles and other traffic?

options.text: Intersections
Highways
Parking lots
Residential streets

questions.explanation: Most conflicts between motorcycles and other traffic happen at intersections. Stay alert where another vehicle might cross in front of you.

questions.question: How much of a motorcycle's stopping power comes from the front brake?

options.text: About one-quarter
About one-half
About three-quarters

questions.explanation: The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake. It provides about three-quarters of a motorcycle's total stopping power.

questions.question: What should a face shield NOT be?

options.text: Scratched
Blocking side views
Airtight
Loose

questions.explanation: A good face shield should be scratch-free, allow clear side views, fasten securely, and let air pass through. An airtight face shield causes fogging and makes it hard to see.

questions.question: Motorcycle riders must wear a helmet by law.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Helmets are not required by law in Illinois, but they are highly recommended. They greatly reduce the risk of a fatal head injury.

questions.question: What should passengers do on a motorcycle?

options.text: Lean when the operator leans.
Hold onto the seat.
Sit as far back as possible.
Never hold onto the operator.

questions.explanation: Passengers should sit directly behind the operator and lean when the operator leans. They should sit as close to the front as possible without crowding the operator and hold onto the operator's waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: When carrying a passenger, what should the motorcyclist tell them to do?

options.text: Sit as far back as possible.
Hold onto the seat.
Put their feet on the muffler.
Get on after the engine has started.

questions.correctAnswerText: Get on after the engine has started.
questions.explanation: Tell your passenger to get on only after you start the engine. They should sit as close to you as possible without crowding you and hold your waist, hips, or belt firmly. Keep both feet on the footrests at all times.

questions.question: What should you do when it starts raining while riding?

options.text: Ride in the center of the lane.
Pull off the road until it stops raining.
Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
Go faster.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: Do not ride in the center of the lane in wet conditions. Instead, ride in the tire tracks left by other cars. The left tire track is often the best choice, but this can change based on traffic.

questions.question: Most motorcycle crashes happen on short trips.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes happen on short trips of less than five miles, often within the first few minutes of riding.

questions.question: What is a good way to handle tailgaters?

options.text: Change lanes and let them pass.
Ignore them.
Use your horn and make rude gestures.
Speed up to increase the distance between you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change lanes and let them pass.
questions.explanation: The best way to handle a tailgater is to change lanes and let them pass. Speeding up makes them tailgate you at a higher speed, which increases danger.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT help lower your chance of a crash?

options.text: Be visible.
Signal your intentions.
Be ready to react to hazards.
Hope another driver sees you.

questions.explanation: To reduce crash risk, be visible and signal your plans clearly. Keep space between you and other vehicles. Scan the road ahead for hazards and be ready to react. Do not rely on hope—take action instead.

questions.question: When riding a motorcycle, which lane position should you use?

options.text: Always avoid the left side of the lane.
Always avoid the right side of the lane.
Always avoid the center of the lane.
Use whichever side is safest for the conditions.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use whichever side is safest for the conditions.
questions.explanation: There is no single lane position to always avoid. Move to different positions based on road conditions.

questions.question: When another vehicle is passing you, where should you ride?

options.text: In the center of the lane.
In the left side of the lane.
In the right side of the lane.
Move between all three parts of the lane as they pass.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the center of the lane.
questions.explanation: When being passed, ride in the center of your lane. Riding near the passing vehicle increases collision risk. Riding far from it may cause them to merge back into your lane too soon.

questions.question: When it starts raining, what should you do?

options.text: Get off the road.
Ride in the tire tracks left by other vehicles.
Ride in the center of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by other vehicles.
questions.explanation: When it rains, do not ride in the center of the lane. Instead, ride in the tire tracks left by vehicles ahead of you. The left tire track is often best, but choose based on traffic and conditions.
